notes: Very widely and consistently attributed to Lucille Ball, usually in the form 'I'd rather regret the things I've done than regret the things I haven't done.' I cannot place a primary interview, memoir passage, or dated print appearance from training knowledge. The sentiment also belongs to a large family of older 'regret what you didn't do' maxims (compare the apocryphal Twain 'Twenty years from now' line), which raises the baseline risk that this was retrofitted onto a famous name. Plausible but unverified.

The IDEA is genuinely Lucretian: De Rerum Natura I.313 has 'stilicidi casus lapidem cavat' — the fall of dripping water hollows the stone. But this specific English wording, with the 'not by violence, but by oft falling' antithesis, is not a standard translation of that line; I recall it as English homiletic phrasing associated with Hugh Latimer's mid-16th-century preaching ('the drop of rain maketh a hole in the stone, not by violence, but by oft falling'). Related but distinct is Ovid's 'gutta cavat lapidem' (Ex Ponto IV.10.5). So the attribution is half-right: Lucretius for the thought, an English preacher's rhetoric for the sentence. Flagging rather than reattributing because my recall of the Latimer wording is good but not certain.

I recall a remark of this shape in Wittgenstein's Culture and Value (Vermischte Bemerkungen), the posthumous collection of personal notebook remarks from the 1930s-40s, running roughly 'When you are frightened of the truth (as I am now) then it is never the whole truth that you have an inkling of.' The 'than' in the corpus text is a transcription corruption of 'that', and the ellipsis marks an elided parenthetical. I am reasonably confident the remark is authentic Wittgenstein but cannot name page or dated entry, so I am not citing a print source and am holding confidence below the promotion bar. Worth a human check against Culture and Value.

M. C. (Mary Caroline) Richards, potter and poet, wrote Centering in Pottery, Poetry, and the Person (1962), The Crossing Point, and Toward Wholeness; this aphorism is stylistically consistent with her work and with Centering's themes of self-formation through craft. I cannot place the line in a specific book or page from training knowledge, and short epigrammatic fragments like this circulate easily without provenance. Attribution is plausible and I have no evidence against it, but nothing supports it either.

This is a modern English distillation of a Buddhist teaching (the second arrow, Sallatha Sutta), not a translation of any canonical text. The 'M. Kathleen Casey' credit propagates through 20th-century recovery and daily-meditation literature and through quote aggregators, but I cannot identify a book, page, or date for it, and Casey herself is a thinly documented figure easily confused with Karen Casey (Each Day a New Beginning, Hazelden). The line was popularized in the wider culture by Haruki Murakami's What I Talk About When I Talk About Running (2007), where he presents it as an anonymous runners' mantra rather than crediting Casey. Attribution is a convention, not evidence.

Circulates under Escher's name in design and business collections, but I know a closely matching line from Miguel de Unamuno — 'Solo el que ensaya lo absurdo es capaz de conquistar lo imposible' / 'Only he who attempts the absurd is capable of achieving the impossible' — which reads as the likelier origin. I cannot place the sentence in Escher's own writings (his essays and letters are fairly well documented and this is not a phrasing I associate with them). My Unamuno recall is solid on the Spanish wording but I cannot name the specific work, so the reattribution is offered as probable, not established, and the Escher attribution should not be promoted.

Macrina Wiederkehr (1939-2020), Benedictine sister and author of A Tree Full of Angels (1988), Seasons of Your Heart, and Behold Your Life. The passage is idiomatically hers — the vocabulary of blessing, presence, and daily decision matches her devotional prose — and I have no reason to doubt the attribution. But I cannot identify which of her books it comes from, and prose excerpts from devotional writers are frequently re-cut and re-punctuated by anthologists. Attribution plausible, source unplaced.

earliest_print_source: A Tree Full of Angels: Seeing the Holy in the Ordinary, Macrina Wiederkehr, 1988
notes: Strong internal evidence: the passage contains both halves of the book's own title — 'Every tree is full of angels' and the seeing-the-holy-in-the-ordinary theme — and theophany-in-the-ordinary is the organizing argument of A Tree Full of Angels (Harper & Row, 1988). This is the single most-anthologized Wiederkehr passage and the attribution is consistent wherever it appears. I am confident in the book but cannot give a page, and I am citing from recall rather than from a copy in front of me, so I am stopping short of 'verified'.

'Maharishi' is a title, not an author — presumably Maharishi Mahesh Yogi is intended, but the corpus entry does not say so, and the passage does not read like his teaching or like translated Indian devotional prose. The idiom is modern American therapeutic-spiritual English ('the ego searches for shortcomings', 'nothing is ever needed but more love') and sits much closer to the A Course in Miracles milieu — Jampolsky, Prather, Williamson and their imitators — than to Vedic commentary. I cannot identify the actual author, and I will not guess one. The attribution as it stands is unusable and the text should not be promoted under this name.

One of the more defensible Gandhi attributions: the sentiment is squarely his (seva as self-realization) and the line is generally treated as sourced in his writings rather than as folk attribution. I cannot name the volume of the Collected Works or the Young India issue, so I am not citing a source. Held at 0.6 rather than higher because Gandhi is a misattribution magnet and 'widely cited with consistent wording' is weaker evidence for him than for almost any other author. Note the corpus text has a typo: 'youself' should be 'yourself'.

The form usually treated as closer to Gandhi is 'The future depends on what we do in the present.' The 'what you do today' version in the corpus is a later, punchier simplification of that, of the kind motivational-poster culture produces. I cannot place either form in a primary Gandhi text. Given how heavily Gandhi's name attracts unsourced aphorisms, and given that this specific wording appears to be a rewrite rather than the earliest form, it should not be promoted.

This is a modern condensation of q_0938 in the same batch ('Man often becomes what he believes himself to be...'), which is the longer and better-documented form of the same passage. The underlying thought is authentically Gandhi's, but this compressed first-person rewrite is not his sentence. Recommend the corpus keep q_0938 and treat this as a duplicate paraphrase rather than a separate quote.

This longer form is the one that appears in serious Gandhi collections and is generally treated as sourced to his own writings, with stable wording across citations — a good sign, since spurious Gandhi lines tend to drift. The prose rhythm ('Man often becomes what he believes himself to be', 'On the contrary...') is consistent with his English. I cannot name the volume of the Collected Works or the periodical and date, so no print source is cited and I am holding just below the promotion bar. A human check against the Collected Works would likely confirm it.

This is the 'thoughts become words, words become actions, habits become values, values become destiny' chain, one of the most durable false Gandhi attributions. No Gandhi source exists for it. Its ancestor is the 19th-century English maxim 'Sow a thought, reap an act; sow an act, reap a habit; sow a habit, reap a character; sow a character, reap a destiny', variously credited to Charles Reade and to Samuel Smiles and itself of contested origin; the modern positive-thinking chain is a 20th-century self-help reworking that later acquired Gandhi's name. I can identify the family the saying descends from but not a single true author, so I am leaving the reattribution null rather than guessing. Should not appear in the corpus under Gandhi.

Ubiquitous under Gandhi's name, especially in slow-living and productivity writing, but I cannot place it in any primary text and I associate it with the unsourced tier of the Gandhi quote literature rather than the documented tier. The epigram's shape — a single modern aphorism about 'speed' — fits mid-to-late 20th-century Western anxieties about pace more naturally than Gandhi's own idiom. Plausible in sentiment, unsupported in provenance.

The documented origin of this formula is the American pacifist A. J. Muste, who said 'There is no way to peace; peace is the way' — a line strongly associated with him in the 1960s and quoted in coverage around his death in 1967. The corpus's 'no path to peace / peace is the path' is a variant of Muste's sentence, and the Gandhi credit appears to be later drift onto a bigger name, a pattern well documented for pacifist aphorisms. I am confident enough in the Muste attribution to name it, though I cannot cite the specific speech or article.

I believe this is authentic Gandhi, from his journalism of the 1920s (the Young India period), and it is one of the Gandhi passages that circulates with a real source trail rather than as a bare aphorism. Two textual notes for the corpus: the authentic wording is 'transmuted', not 'transmitted' — the corpus text has the corruption twice, which flattens the heat/energy metaphor — and 'a power which can move the world' is the more usual ending. Recommend correcting to 'transmuted' before any promotion. Not citing a dated source because I cannot pin the issue.

Well attested by the standards of Gandhi quotation. The line comes with a consistent anecdote — Gandhi, pressed by a journalist for a message and having no time to talk, wrote 'My life is my message' on a scrap of paper — and it is established enough to have been used as the title of Narayan Desai's multi-volume Gandhi biography. I cannot fix the date or the journalist with confidence, so no print source is cited, but the attribution itself is solid.

Consistently attributed to Gandhi with stable wording, and I associate it with his own writing rather than with the aggregator tier — the balanced construction ('the strongest might weaken and the wisest might err') and the theme of humility before one's own certainty are characteristic. It appears in the standard Gandhi anthologies of the All Men Are Brothers type. I cannot name the original article or speech, so it stays below the promotion bar pending a check against the Collected Works.

The single most famous thing Gandhi never said in these words. No source exists in his writings or speeches. The genuine passage it compresses is 'If we could change ourselves, the tendencies in the world would also change. As a man changes his own nature, so does the attitude of the world change towards him' — a different and more careful claim. The imperative-slogan wording appears to originate in 1970s American self-help; Arleen Lorrance's The Love Project material (c. 1974) carried 'Be the change you want to see happen', and the Gandhi credit attached later. Brian Morton's widely read 2011 New York Times piece 'Falser Words Were Never Spoken' laid this out. I name Lorrance as probable origin of the phrasing, but the sentiment is a fair paraphrase of Gandhi, so the corpus may prefer to carry the authentic longer passage instead. Do not promote under Gandhi as written.
suggested_reattribution: Arleen Lorrance (probable origin of the wording); the underlying sentiment paraphrases Gandhi

notes: Extremely widely quoted — it is a fixture of animal-welfare campaigning — but I know it as one of the Gandhi lines for which no source in the Collected Works has been located, and it is commonly listed in the unsourced or disputed tier of Gandhi quotation. Related sentiments do appear in his writing on cow protection and ahimsa, which is likely how the attribution took hold. Ubiquity here is a function of the cause it serves, not of evidence.

Reads as authentic: it is long, syntactically unpolished, argumentative rather than epigrammatic, and it develops a thought about seva step by step — all features that spurious Gandhi quotes lack, since fabrications tend to be short and quotable. The wording is stable across the citations I recall. I cannot place the source text, so this is a judgment from style and internal evidence rather than from provenance, and I am keeping it below the promotion bar until someone checks the Collected Works.

The pre-flag is correct. No Gandhi source exists. The earliest credited appearances run through mid-20th-century secondary literature — Louis Fischer's The Life of Mahatma Gandhi (1950) carries a version of the thought as biographer's paraphrase rather than as a transcribed Gandhi sentence — and the line reached mass currency through Attenborough's Gandhi (1982), which drew on Fischer. The underlying reversal of lex talionis is older than Gandhi and circulated independently in English. Fischer is the likeliest proximate source of the wording, but as a paraphraser rather than an author, so I am recording that in notes rather than naming him as the quote's author.

Generally treated as authentic Gandhi and traced to his periodical writing of the early 1930s; the wording is stable across citations and the aphorism-plus-gloss structure matches his editorial style. I cannot name the issue or date, so no print source is given. Held at 0.62 for the standing Gandhi caution — the line is short and quotable, the profile of quotes that drift — but I have no positive evidence against it.

Not a canonical translation. The Majjhima Nikaya credit points at a 152-sutta collection without naming a sutta, and this English does not match any translation tradition I know — not Horner, not Nanamoli/Bodhi. Telltales: 'illusion that he is a permanent self' is a doctrinal gloss on anatta in modern comparative-religion register, not sutta idiom, and the sutta form (address to named interlocutors, formulaic repetition, similes) is entirely absent. This reads as a Western summary of Buddhist teaching later given a scriptural label — a common pattern in inspirational anthologies. Treat the citation as decorative; I cannot identify the actual writer.
